doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Crowley family, Professor O'Jay and Illinois Jacquet
summary: Jordan's family was not very musical; his teacher Professor O'Jay taught Illinois Jacquet, and Jacquet's honking and screaming opened Jordan to playing free and high notes.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I’m constantly amazed by the family traditions in New Orleans. And we’ll talk maybe later about your children. But was your family, your parents, your siblings, were they as musical as your kids?

No they wasn’t. They, in fact my father now, I didn’t come from New Orleans, I came from a little town they called Crowley, Louisiana. And he had some cousins that played. But my daddy used to get, on a Saturday night sometimes when he had a few little drinks in him, he would pick up accordion and try to keep up with them. But they played guitar and bass, his cousins, our cousins. So they had a band but he would try, but if he didn’t have a few drinks in him he wouldn’t even deal with it at all other than the radio. Now we used to listen to the radio quite a bit. And all my brothers and sisters, there’s one time they played in the band, we was in a Catholic school. And they had a very important teacher in my town, Professor O’Jay. He came from the Canadian Conservatory. He was a hell of a trumpet player. And he taught everybody in that area. In fact he taught Illinois Jacquet. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Illinois. He told me, he say you were my, well the old man was old and he say, “you’re my last good student.” And he used to tell me, I loved horses. And he used to tell me Illinois Jacquet used to ride from Cade, Louisiana to his house on a horse. And I used to, he’d tell me about Illinois’ horse, and I loved horses. I still love them. So he used to tell me about that. And so this is one of the real things, and he’d be hyping me up with Illinois and I’d be playing anything, say hell you so and so and so. So he used that to hype me up with. And then later on I got a chance when I first got the glimpse of playing free was with Illinois Jacquet honking and screaming. See like a lot of people think you know, but when I heard that I said now this could go another way. And I started dealing with freedom you know, like playing free. Because when you’re honking and screaming and going on it can give you ideas and at that time the people couldn’t play the high notes on the saxophone like we do now. So when I was in high school I could play the high notes on the saxophone, I could play an octave over F. So that would just open the way for me to go on into something else because I was hearing the upper registers.
